entries.title: A Prop 65 Crash Course: What You Need to Know (2026)
entries.summary: If you see a Prop 65 warning, don’t fret. Here’s what you need to know.
entries.content:
My first encounter with a Prop 65 warning was on the back of my TV.

I was selling it on Facebook Marketplace, and when the buyer arrived to pick it up, he spotted a warning I had never noticed. “California Proposition 65 Warning: This product contains chemicals known to the state of California to cause cancer and birth defects or reproductive harm.” Neither of us had seen such a label before, and for a moment, he didn’t want the TV anymore. We did what anyone would do in this situation: We Googled it. He ended up taking the TV. I kept Googling.

California’s Proposition 65, officially called the Safe Drinking Water and Toxic Enforcement Act, applies to a dizzying range of products, from food and cosmetics to electronics and household goods. Passed in 1986, the law turns 40 this year, yet that ominous little label still confuses the average consumer.

So, should you steer clear of all products with a Prop 65 warning? Not necessarily. Here’s what you need to know before you panic-buy a new TV.

Proposition 65, Explained

In November 1986, California voters approved Proposition 65 by a landslide margin of about 63 percent to 37 percent. It’s a right-to-know law, meant to inform Californians about potential exposure to chemicals that may cause cancer or reproductive harm over a lifetime.

It doesn’t ban those chemicals; instead, it requires businesses to provide a warning when their products could expose people to a listed chemical at levels above specific thresholds.

“At that time, it was part of a broader effort to address a growing concern that the public had about toxic chemical exposure,” says Megan Schwarzman, environmental health scientist at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health.

The idea is that consumers can use that information to make their own decisions. A warning might prompt someone to choose an alternative, use a product less frequently, or take other steps to reduce their exposure. Prop 65 also gives businesses an incentive to reformulate products or change manufacturing practices to avoid issuing a warning that may deter customers.

And because California is such a massive consumer market, products often need to comply with Prop 65 requirements even when they’re manufactured or sold by companies elsewhere. Some large retailers, such as Target and Amazon, also require their vendors to comply with Prop 65 warning requirements.

Prop 65 Is Everywhere

Prop 65 covers a broad range of products and potential exposures. You can find warnings on fortified foods, smartphones, and appliances. The law is concerned with exposure, not simply whether the chemical is detectable. California's Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA) establishes the so-called safe-harbor levels for many listed chemicals. Generally speaking, a warning is required when anticipated exposure exceeds these levels.

The Prop 65 list contains both naturally occurring and synthetic chemicals that California has determined are known to cause cancer or reproductive harm. Supplements, for example, can contain trace amounts of naturally occurring or environmental contaminants, including lead, cadmium, and arsenic. The list is updated at least annually, and chemicals can also be removed from the list as scientific evidence evolves.

Chemicals can be added to the Prop 65 list through four mechanisms: through California’s Labor Code; through evaluations from California’s Carcinogen Identification Committee (CIC) or Developmental and Reproductive Toxicant Identification Committee (DARTIC); through identification by certain authoritative bodies, like the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA); or through identification by a state or federal agency.

Mariana C. Stern, cancer epidemiologist and member of the CIC, says the committee includes epidemiologists, toxicologists, molecular biologists, and cancer scientists who review the available literature before deciding whether a chemical belongs on the list.

“We may spend the whole day trying to dissect one chemical,” Stern says. “It’s not uncommon that we end up deciding we don’t have enough evidence to add this compound to the list.”

But seeing a warning doesn’t necessarily mean a product contains a dangerous amount of a chemical, or even that the product itself has been tested. According to Schwarzman, “some companies have opted to warn rather than test or reformulate, but from our research, I believe that is much less common than when companies post a warning because of the actual presence of the chemical above a certain threshold.”

From a consumer standpoint, the ubiquity of Prop 65 labels also means that it can be harder to prioritize which ones actually warrant attention. “We definitely have a concern with over-warning,” says Tina Cox, section chief of the OEHHA’s Proposition 65 Implementation Program. “Any unnecessary warnings do make it difficult for consumers to identify where the real exposures are, and it does dilute the value of Prop 65 warnings.”

As a result, California has started trying to make them more useful by requiring short-form warnings to name at least one chemical, rather than relying on the generic “may cause cancer or reproductive harm” language. Businesses have until January 2028 to fully comply with the new requirement. The state is also conducting more outreach to help companies understand when a warning is required and when it is not.

The Warning Isn’t a Verdict

Prop 65 was meant to inform consumers, not to tell them which products to buy. By the same token, a product without a warning isn’t necessarily free of hazardous chemicals.

“You’re never going to be zero exposure, even if you avoid all Prop 65 labels,” says air pollution scientist Shahir Fouad Masri. “If you have a product that doesn’t have a label, it’s one of two things: It was tested and it didn’t exceed Prop 65, and therefore it’s safe, or simply nobody ever sent it to the lab.”

That said, a Prop 65 warning is still useful information, and there are ways to reduce your exposure to these harmful chemicals. “Everybody has different risk tolerances and different priorities,” says Schwarzman. Consider how frequently you use the product and at what dose.

“Exposure from that one product, in many cases, is not going to cause cancer,” adds Cox, “but maybe over a lifetime of exposure, or exposure to similar products that have the same chemical, will increase your risk for cancer or reproductive toxicity.”

One example is holiday lights. Flexible plastic components can contain phthalates, which are added to PVC (polyvinyl chloride) to make it more pliable. Those chemicals migrate out of the plastic and come into contact with your hands or enter household dust. “My own choice around that is to handle them briefly and wash my hands,” says Schwarzman. “I don’t have my kids handle them, and I do make a different decision about that than something I’d be consuming on a daily basis.”

On a similar note, if you’re concerned about a warning on a tool, Masri suggests wearing gloves to reduce direct skin contact. There’s also a difference in dermal absorption rate. The skin on your hands, for example, is generally thicker and more calloused than the skin on your face, which means less absorption. So you might think differently about a screwdriver you occasionally handle with gloves than an LED mask you put directly on your face every day, where the potential for absorption is higher.

TL;DR

If you’re considering a product with a Prop 65 warning, don’t fret. Instead, look for more information.

  • Determine what chemical triggered the warning, if identified.
  • Check whether the manufacturer provides testing or contaminant information. Look for credible third-party certification, where appropriate.
  • Consider how frequently you’re using the product and how extensively. Occasional exposure is different from using something every day.
  • Don’t assume the absence of a Prop 65 label means the product is free of contaminants.
  • For consumers who want to dig deeper, P65warnings.ca.gov has information about individual chemicals and ways to reduce exposure. There’s also a dedicated Help Desk for Prop 65, along with an email and phone line for specific inquiries.
  • If you’re pregnant, trying to become pregnant, taking medications, or managing a medical condition, talk to a qualified health professional.

Prop 65 is a right-to-know law meant to raise awareness and ensure that we, as consumers, have an impact on the type of products we’re exposed to in our daily lives. As Schwarzman puts it, “I want to encourage us all not to feel like the toxic things are inevitable, and there’s nothing we can do, because there often is something we can do.”

Meet the Experts

  • Tina Cox, senior environmental scientist (supervisory) and section chief of the Proposition 65 Implementation Program at the Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA)
  • Mariana C. Stern, PhD, a cancer epidemiologist and professor of preventive medicine and urology at the University of Southern California, Keck School of Medicine
  • Megan Schwarzman, MD, a physician and environmental health scientist at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health
  • Shahir Fouad Masri, ScD, an air pollution scientist at the University of California, Irvine

entries.title: Hoka Coupon Codes: 30% Off in September 2026
entries.summary: Unlock free expedited shipping or 10% off with today’s Hoka discount codes, plus save up to 30% with the best discounts for September 2026.
entries.content:
If you’ve been outside since 2020, you’ve probably noticed Hoka. You may even own a pair, too. The once-niche running shoe brand has gone from a favorite among trail and mountain runners to an everyday fixture on sidewalks, running paths, and airports. Founded in 2009, Hoka built its reputation on plush cushioning and oversized midsoles, which is an aesthetic that has since become difficult to miss.

The Clifton is our iconic go-to for everyday running, while the Speedgoat series is our favorite for trail running. The latter is cushioned enough for long miles, with enough responsiveness and control to handle technical terrain. Its grip is excellent, too, making it an all-arounder rather than a shoe reserved for a particular type of trail. For hiking, we love Hoka’s more rugged Anacapa line.

Hoka shoes aren’t exactly cheap, so I’ve rounded up the best Hoka promo codes and Hoka coupons to help you save on your next pair.

Get 10% Off Your Next Order With Hoka Coupon Code

Hoka wants to reward you for purchases you’re already making (for yourself or the runner in your life). When you join the Hoka membership, you’ll get 10% off your next purchase. All you need to do is sign up with your email online, and a unique, single use Hoka coupon code will be sent via email after you register. Just copy and paste the special code for savings on your favorite sneakers.

Unlock a Hoka Discount Code For Free Expedited Shipping

If you’ve never bought Hokas before (and if not, why not?), new customers get free expedited shipping on the first order when they sign up for emails and texts. It’s worth noting here that this Hoka promo code only applies if you are a new customer and you need to register both your email address and your phone number for texts to receive the Hoka coupon code.

To get the Hoka discount code, enter your email address in the pop-up window, and then your mobile phone number. To subscribe, reply Y. Another text will be sent, with a single-use code for free expedited shipping. You can then receive notifications of new shoe releases, limited edition styles, and flash sales. (The all-new Kaha 2 Frost Moc is waterproof for what promises to be a very wet winter for some of us.)

Save up to 30% on Our Favorite Hoka Running Shoes

Don’t know which shoes to buy? Let us help you out. Hoka regularly offers up to 30 percent off on its bestsellers (check out the rotating markdowns here).

Take advantage of these Hoka discount codes and hit the trails. Some of the best Hoka deals we’ve seen recently are 30% off Speedgoat 6 trail running and hiking shoes at $47 off, now $108; 20% off the Mach 6, a solid pair of everyday running shoes at $28 off; and 20% off the Clifton 10, another popular everyday running or walking tennis shoe, now $31 off (only $124 total). Plus, you can get 20% off the Bondi 9, another uber-popular everyday running or walking shoe at $35 off, and a whopping 30% off Transport hiking/walking shoes at $45 off.

Hoka Student Discount: 15% Off

Hoka knows that those who help others are on their feet a lot deserve comfort and style as they devote their time to the rest of us. That’s why Hoka offers discounts for medical workers, first responders, students, teachers, military, and veterans. To get your Hoka promo code or Hoka discount, once your items are in the cart, verify through ID.me with the ID.me button. Then, follow the steps to complete the verification process and watch the savings roll in. Plus, Hoka even categorizes its styles that are best for medical workers, best for first responders, and best for students and teachers, based on each’s particular needs as it pertains to their profession.

Save 10% on Your Next Pair of Hoka Clifton 10s

If you’re an avid runner or just want to upgrade your footwear this season, investing in a Hoka membership (more on that below) is the best way to save on future purchases longterm. A Hoka membership will get you 10% off bestselling shoes, like Hoka Clifton 10 womens and Hoka men's Clifton 10 styles.

Get 30% Off Hoka Outlet Sale

One of the best ways to save big is with the short-lived Hoka Outlet. This is a limited run, open exclusively for Hoka newsletter subscribers. If you sign up now to receive Hoka newsletters, you’ll be able to get up to 30% off selected styles for the outlet sale. Just know that this Hoka discount is for selected styles only, and ends September 20.

Hoka Members Get Free Shipping and Extended Returns

If you opt to join Hoka’s free membership program, you automatically receive free standard shipping on every order and you’ll automatically qualify for free shipping if you’re logged into your account.

More Hoka Membership Perks

Hoka’s guaranteed “Fly for 30” program means that everyone who buys a pair of Hoka shoes gets a 30-day trial. You can then return the shoes or exchange them for a different size, style, or color. However, Hoka members get access to the Fly for 60 program, which is an extended 2-month guaranteed return window.

You also get access to Hoka’s exclusive events, run clubs, and sweepstakes (check to see if your city is a featured city here). You will also be the first to hear about new promotions and discounts.

Don’t Miss 10% Off Hoka Trail Shoes

As mentioned, if you’re an avid runner, Hoka’s membership is a great way to save big on purchases you were already going to make. With a Hoka membership, you’ll get 10% off bestselling styles, from the Hoka Speedgoat 7 for the trailrunner, to the hiking Transport 2, there’s a Hoka shoe for every type of terrain and runner (now for less!).
